Rarefaction curves showed that neurotypical individuals had a higher number of observed bacterial species than autistic individuals (Figure 1A and Figure S1). As an alternative method to estimate the richness, we employed the nonparametric Chao1 estimator in various levels of OTU clustering. Similar to the rarefaction data from observed OTUs, the neurotypical group had significantly higher number of estimated OTUs (Figure 1B and Table S2A), which indicates that the neurotypical group had higher bacterial richness than the autistic group. entities.context: Different from the Shannon index, the PD index incorporates the concept of phylogenetic distinctiveness and is sensitive to species relatedness by summing the tree-branch length present in each subject of a phylogenetic dendrogram . The PD index revealed that the neurotypical group harbored more diverse gut microbiota than the autistic group did (P,0.05 by one- tailed Mann-Whitney test in Figure 1C and Table S2D). In addition, we also evaluated correlation between bacterial richness/ diversity and the severity of GI problems within the autistic group, and bacterial richness was negatively correlated with GI severity (Table S3). Taken together, these analyses suggest that the presence of autistic symptoms and their correlated GI problems are linked with reduced richness and diversity of gut microflora, which results in a decrease in microbial redundancy and alter the physiological functionality and microbial GI robustness in children with ASD.

entities.definition: A genus of bacteria commonly found in the human gut microbiota.

entities.context: By pyrosequencing the V2/V3 regions in bacterial 16S rDNA from fecal DNA samples, we compared gut microbiomes of GI symptom-free neurotypical children with those of autistic children mostly presenting GI symptoms. Unexpectedly, the presence of autistic symptoms, rather than the severity of GI symptoms, was associated with less diverse gut microbiomes. Further, rigorous statistical tests with multiple testing corrections showed significantly lower abundances of the genera Prevotella, Coprococcus, and unclassified Veillonellaceae in autistic samples. These are intriguingly versatile carbohydrate- degrading and/or fermenting bacteria, suggesting a potential influence of unusual diet patterns observed in autistic children. However, multivariate analyses showed that autism-related changes in both overall diversity and individual genus abundances were correlated with the presence of autistic symptoms but not with their diet patterns.
entities.definition: A genus of anaerobic bacteria associated with gut fermentation.

entities.context: In addition, considering the potential interactions between intestinal microbes and the central nervous system , abnormal intestinal flora may be associated not only with GI problems but also with ASD-related behavioral symptoms. Potential involvement of gut microbes in ASD etiology has been speculated for more than a decade. Many pathogenic gram- negative bacteria contain lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in their cell walls, which can cause damage in various tissues including the brain . LPS-induced inflammation in the brain increases permeability of the blood-brain barrier and facilitates an accumulation of high levels of mercury in cerebrum, which may aggravate ASD symptoms . A test in rats showed that prenatal LPS exposure decreased levels of glutathione , which is an important antioxidant involved in heavy metal detoxification in the brain.
entities.definition: A component of Gram-negative bacterial cell walls that triggers immune responses.

entities.context: Therefore, here we aimed to define systemic changes in gut microbiome associated with autism and autism-related GI problems. We recruited 20 neurotypical and 20 autistic children accompanied by a survey of both autistic severity and GI symptoms. By pyrosequencing the V2/V3 regions in bacterial 16S rDNA from fecal DNA samples, we compared gut microbiomes of GI symptom-free neurotypical children with those of autistic children mostly presenting GI symptoms. Unexpectedly, the presence of autistic symptoms, rather than the severity of GI symptoms, was associated with less diverse gut microbiomes. Further, rigorous statistical tests with multiple testing corrections showed significantly lower abundances of the genera Prevotella, Coprococcus, and unclassified Veillonellaceae in autistic samples.

bioprojects.title: A pilot integrative analysis of colonic gene expression, gut microbiota and immune infiltration in primary sclerosing cholangitis-inflammatory bowel disease: association of disease with bile acid pathways
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the pathophysiological differences between PSC-IBD and UC through a comparative integrative analysis of colonic gene expression, microbiota, and immune infiltration. Using shotgun RNA-seq, 16S rRNA profiling, and immunophenotyping, it identifies distinct transcriptomic and microbial signatures in PSC-IBD, including upregulation of bile acid pathways and immune responses. The research highlights dysregulated bile acid homeostasis in PSC-IBD compared to UC, suggesting novel therapeutic targets.

entities.context: 25 Bile acid regulation is mediated through a negative feedback mechanism as part of its enterohepatic recirculation by hormones such as fibroblast growth factor (FGF) 15 (murine) and 19 (human). Bile acids are reabsorbed primarily by terminal ileal enterocytes and partly by colonocytes. This activates FXR (farnesoid X receptor) by upregulation of the FGF15/19 pathway which consequently leads to inhibition of hepatic bile acids synthesis through suppression of CYP7A1 enzyme. We have shown that multiple nuclear receptors specifically FXR (NR1H4), PXR (pregnane X receptor) and PPAR- γ (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma) are upregulated in PSC-IBD compared to UC. As bile acids are inherently cytotoxic, these nuclear receptors, in particular FXR, a bile acid-activated transcriptional factor, may be activated in order to induce gene expression circuitry to protect against bile acid toxicity by shutting down expression of genes that increase influx and synthesis of bile.

entities.context: We sought to define further the pathophysiologic differences in PSC-IBD and UC, by applying a comparative and integrative approach in this pilot study. Methods: Colonic biopsies were collected from patients with PSC-IBD (n=10), UC (n=10) and healthy controls (HC; n=10). Results: The colonic transcriptome differed significantly between groups (P=0.01).

bioprojects.title: Alterations in Oral Microbiota in HIV are Related to Decreased Pulmonary Function
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the relationship between oral microbiota alterations in HIV-positive individuals and decreased pulmonary function. Using 16S rRNA sequencing of saliva and stool samples from PWH and HIV-uninfected controls, the research identifies distinct oral microbial communities associated with HIV status and smoking. The study finds that altered oral microbiomes correlate with reduced lung function metrics (FEV1/FVC, DLco) in PWH, suggesting a potential role of the oral microbiome in HIV-related COPD pathogenesis. No significant gut microbiome associations were observed.

entities.context: As in previous work, the oral microbiome of PWH differed from that of HIV- uninfected individuals (13, 15, 51). PWH had decreased oral microbiome alpha diversity, and there were differences in beta diversity when compared to HIV-uninfected controls. The LHMP compared the oral and lung microbiome of PWH to HIV-uninfected individuals and reported increased abundance of oral Streptococcus, Actinomyces and Rothia in PWH (14). Our results were similar in identifying increases in oral Veillonella, Rothia, Streptococcus and decreased Neisseria in PWH. Prior work also reported decreased oral microbial alpha diversity in PWH with low CD4 counts after 24 weeks of ART (52).

The lung is exposed to the oral microbiome via microaspiration, and changes in the oral microbiome may impact lung disease.

entities.context: What This Study Adds to the Field: We performed bacterial 16S rRNA sequencing of saliva and stool in the Pittsburgh site of the Multicenter AIDS cohort study (MACS) of PWH and HIV-uninfected individuals, with and without COPD. We identified oral microbiome differences by HIV and smoking status. We discovered a novel association of oral microbiome to lung function measured by post- bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in one second/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) or reduced diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLco). There were no significant relationships of stool microbiome to lung function. This study suggests that the oral microbiome may play an important role in HIV COPD pathogenesis, possibly by stimulating inflammation and promoting lung damage.

Although the similarity of lung and oral samples has previously been shown, there is not 100% overlap and the fact that we found alterations in the oral microbiome associated with HIV, smoking, and lung function that have not been reported in the lung suggest that there are important differences. These differences may occur even if the oral microbiome is largely responsible for populating the lung microbiome as bronchoalveolar lavage dilutes bacterial communities which may render the bacteria below the limit of detection, and aspiration of oral microbes is likely intermittent and could be missed during a single bronchoscopy. Finally, we performed 16S sequencing, and it is possible that whole genome sequencing or metatranscriptomics might have uncovered additional differences in these populations. bioprojects.title: Short-term supplementation of celecoxib-shifted butyrate production on a simulated model of the gut microbial ecosystem and ameliorated in vitro inflammation
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates how short-term celecoxib exposure affects gut microbiota metabolism and inflammation. Using in vitro models, it shows that celecoxib alters bacterial fermentation, reduces butyrate production, and modulates inflammatory markers like IL-8. The research highlights bidirectional interactions between drugs and the microbiome, emphasizing their role in drug efficacy and safety.

bioprojects.title: Progressive Shifts in the Gut Microbiome Reﬂect Prediabetes and Diabetes Development in a Treatment-Naive Mexican Cohort
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the relationship between gut microbiome changes and Type 2 diabetes (T2D) progression in a treatment-naive Mexican cohort. Using clinical data from 405 individuals, it identifies specific bacterial genera correlated with T2D risk factors like blood glucose levels and beta cell dysfunction. The research demonstrates that metformin treatment can restore the gut microbiome to a normoglycemic state. It highlights the importance of controlling for confounding variables like obesity and comorbidities, providing evidence for the gut microbiome's role in T2D etiology.

Elizabeth Tejero1, Eric Alm4, Osbaldo Resendis-Antonio1,5* and Rodolfo Guardado-Mendoza3,6* 1 Computational Genomics, Instituto Nacional de Medicina Geno´ mica (INMEGEN), Mexico City, Mexico,2 Gibbons Lab, Institute for Systems Biology, Seattle, WA, United States,3 Metabolic Research Laboratory, Department of Medicine and Nutrition, University of Guanajuato, Leo´ n, Mexico,4 Center for Microbiome Informatics and Therapeutics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, United States,5 Human Systems Biology Laboratory, Coordinacio´ nd el a Investigacio´ n Cientı´ﬁca—Red de Apoyo a la Investigacio´ n, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM), Mexico City, Mexico, 6 Research Department, Hospital Regional de Alta Especialidad del Bajı´o, Leo´ n, Mexico Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a global epidemic that affects more than 8% of the world’s population and is a leading cause of death in Mexico. Diet and lifestyle are known to contribute to the onset of T2D. However, the role of the gut microbiome in T2D progression remains uncertain.
entities.definition: A metabolic disorder characterized by hyperglycemia due to insulin resistance or beta cell dysfunction

entities.context: Associations between gut bacteria and more than 200 clinical variables revealed a de ﬁned set of bacterial genera that were consistent biomarkers of T2D prevalence and risk. Speciﬁcally, gradual increases in blood glucose levels, beta cell dysfunction, and the accumulation of measured T2D risk factors were correlated with the relative abundances of four bacterial genera. In a cohort of 25 individuals, T2D treatment— predominantly metformin— reliably returned the microbiome to the normoglycemic community state. Deep clinical characterization allowed us to broadly control for confounding variables, indicating that these microbiome patterns were independent of common T2D comorbidities, like obesity or cardiovascular disease. Our work provides theﬁrst solid evidence for a direct link between the gut microbiome and T2D in a critically high-risk population.

entities.context: Most of those have suggested that the diabetic microbiome is less ef ﬁcient in producing short-chain fatty acids (SCFA) due to a loss of butyrate-producing genera (17– 19). However, especially when looking across different populations, the bacterial genera associated with diabetes vary (17), which is consistent with ﬁndings that the gut microbiome composition varies greatly across populations ( 20). For example, an increase of Proteobacteria in T2D was reported for Chinese cohorts but was absent in a European cohort ( 15, 16). Finding robust associations between the microbiome and T2D is further confounded by treatment effects and comorbidities. Metformin, one of the most common medications for T2D, has been shown to modify the gut microbiome which may contribute to its mechanism of action ( 21, 22).

entities.context: T2D incidence is progressively increasing in the Mexican population and has become a major burden for the national health system and one of the leading causes of death in Mexico ( 8– 10). The particular vulnerability of the Mexican population to this disease is driven by general factors such as a sedentary lifestyle and diet but is also in ﬂuenced by genetic risk factors that are enriched in the Mexican population ( 11). For instance, it has been shown that about half of all native Mexicans carry an SLC16A11 variant that increases T2D risk by 20% for each haplotype ( 12– 14). Consequently, there is an urgent need for diagnosis and treatment strategies to limit the progression of T2D in the Mexican high-risk population. Recently, the gut microbiome has been proposed as an important modulator in the progression of T2D.

entities.context: Recently, the gut microbiome has been proposed as an important modulator in the progression of T2D. Several studies have reported a wide array of associations between the gut microbiome and diabetes in European, American, and Chinese cohorts ( 15, 16). Most of those have suggested that the diabetic microbiome is less ef ﬁcient in producing short-chain fatty acids (SCFA) due to a loss of butyrate-producing genera (17– 19). However, especially when looking across different populations, the bacterial genera associated with diabetes vary (17), which is consistent with ﬁndings that the gut microbiome composition varies greatly across populations ( 20). For example, an increase of Proteobacteria in T2D was reported for Chinese cohorts but was absent in a European cohort ( 15, 16).

For this particular study, 470 participants who had an anth ropometric, nutritional, biochemical, and metabolic evaluation, as well as a stool sample collection, were included; at the end, we had complete data and microbiome composition only for 427. For instance, we do not ﬁnd a depletion of the butyrate- producing Roseburia, Faecalibacterium,o r Eubacterium (18) but rather observe a decrease in Anaerostipes hadrus, another known butyrate-producer ( 47). Some studies have also reported an increase of E. coli (15, 16), however, we do not observe an increase in Lactobacillus or Streptococcus as reported there.

bioprojects.title: Amplicon sequencing provides more accurate microbiome information in healthy children compared to culturing
bioprojects.summary: This study compares the diagnostic efficiency of amplicon sequencing and traditional culture methods (TCMs) for analyzing microbiomes in healthy children. Using 3,538 samples (1,748 fecal and 1,790 hypopharyngeal), it found that NGS identified 75.7% of bacterial species cultured by TCMs, while TCMs only detected 23.86%. The paper discusses the pros/cons of both methods and highlights NGS's advantages in microbial diversity but notes TCMs still provide clinical value.

entities.context: Since NGS is more sensitive than traditional culture methods (TCMs), many studies have argued for them to replace TCMs. However, are we really ready for this transition? Here we compare the diagnostic efﬁciency of the two methods using a large number of samples (n = 1,748 fecal and n = 1,790 hypopharyngeal), among healthy children at different time points. Here we show that bacteria identiﬁed by NGS represented 75.70% of the unique bacterial species cultured in each sample, while TCM only identiﬁed 23.86% of the bacterial species found by amplicon sequencing. entities.context: DNA extraction and 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing was done in the same way as published in our earlier studies21. Primers were removed from the MiSeq generated FASTQ ﬁles by cutadapt22. Further, reads were analyzed by QIIME223 pipeline using DADA224 to create sequencing error proﬁles, trim (ﬁrst 8 bp of each read), truncate (forward reads to 180 bp, reverse reads to 160 bp), assemble read pairs, remove chimeras, infer the amplicon sequence var- iants (ASVs) present and assign taxonomy using a pre-trained Naive Bayes clas- siﬁer [Silva Ref NR 99 (release 132)]25. Based on the rarefaction curves for observed richness and Shannon diversity index (Supplementary Fig. 3), samples with <2,000 reads were excluded from the analysis, as well as 3 samples with an unusually high richness, which were suspected to be technical artifacts.
entities.definition: A software tool for denoising amplicon sequencing data

bioprojects.title: A library of human gut bacterial isolates paired with longitudinal multiomics data enables mechanistic microbiome research
bioprojects.summary: This paper introduces the Broad Institute-OpenBiome Microbiome Library (BIO-ML), a comprehensive collection of 7,758 gut bacterial isolates from healthy fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) donors. The study emphasizes the importance of longitudinal multiomics data for understanding microbial stability and dynamics within hosts. Key findings include stable population sizes across humans, reliability of 'omics' methods with multiple sampling days, and associations between gut metabolites and amino acid/bile acid levels. The BIO-ML serves as a resource for mechanistic microbiome research and therapeutic development.

bioprojects.title: Disrupted Maturation of the Microbiota and Metabolome Among Extremely Preterm Infants with Postnatal Growth Failure
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates postnatal growth failure in extremely preterm infants, identifying disrupted intestinal microbiota maturation (low diversity, pathogen dominance) and elevated serum metabolites linked to lipolysis. Machine learning revealed delayed microbiota/metabolome development in growth-failed infants. The research highlights novel microbial and metabolic targets for intervention.
bioprojects.study_title: Disrupted Maturation of the Microbiota and Metabolome Among Extremely Preterm Infants with Postnatal Growth Failure
bioprojects.sample_source: Neonatal intensive care unit (NICU)
bioprojects.health_status: Postnatal growth failure, late-onset sepsis, necrotizing enterocolitis
bioprojects.experimental_design: Longitudinal, prospective cohort study of EPT infants during NICU hospitalization
bioprojects.funding_sources: Gerber Foundation, NIH (K12 HD043494)
bioprojects.confounding_factors: Medical complications (sepsis, NEC), nutritional management
bioprojects.host_age: Median birth gestational age of 26 weeks (IQR: 24–27)
bioprojects.statistical_models: Machine learning algorithms for normal maturation
bioprojects.study_limitations: Potential confounding by medical morbidities and limited sample size

entities.context: Ashley1 Growth failure during infancy is a major global problem that has adverse effects on long-term health and neurodevelopment. Preterm infants are disproportionately affected by growth failure and its effects. Herein we found that extremely preterm infants with postnatal growth failure have disrupted maturation of the intestinal microbiota, characterized by persistently low diversity, dominance of pathogenic bacteria within the Enterobacteriaceae family, and a paucity of strictly anaerobic taxa including Veillonella relative to infants with appropriate postnatal growth. Metabolomic profiling of infants with growth failure demonstrated elevated serum acylcarnitines, fatty acids, and other byproducts of lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation. Machine learning algorithms for normal maturation of the microbiota and metabolome among infants with appropriate growth revealed a pattern of delayed maturation of the microbiota and metabolome among infants with growth failure.
entities.definition: A family of Gram-negative bacteria commonly found in the gut microbiota

entities.context: Other studies provide testable models of how the altered microbiota in growth failure may modulate met- abolic maturity. Studies in gnotobiotic models have shown that the microbiota alters both nutrient extraction and host genes involved in regulating energy expenditure, including fatty acid oxidation27,28. Differences in the functions of the microbiota and the production of bioactive metabolites by the microbiota in growth failure may have effects on host metabolism, as microbial metabolites such as the short-chain fatty acids have a role in regulating glucose homeostasis and lipid metabolism29,30. Differences in innate immune responses to the altered microbiota in growth failure represent another potential mediator of the microbiota-metabolome associations observed in our study. For example, the high burden of Enterobacteriaceae in growth failure may have led to increased inflammation through toll-like receptor 4 activation, which could in turn decrease insulin sensitivity and increase lipolysis markers, since insulin suppresses lipolysis in adipose tissue31.

bioprojects.title: Microbial and metabolomic profiles in correlation with depression and anxiety co-morbidities in diarrhoea-predominant IBS patients
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates microbial and metabolomic changes in diarrhoea-predominant IBS (IBS-D) patients with depression and anxiety. It found altered gut microbiota, including reduced Faecalibacterium and increased Prevotella, along with specific urinary metabolites associated with psychological symptoms. Correlation analyses linked microbial abundance and metabolite levels to IBS severity, anxiety, and depression.
bioprojects.study_title: Microbial and metabolomic profiles in correlation with depression and anxiety co-morbidities in diarrhoea-predominant IBS patients

bioprojects.study_limitations: Inconsistent results in existing literature and limited combination of microbiome/metabolomic data in IBS studies.

In comparison, urine was much easier to obtain at an outpatient clinic, considered sterile, and free from bio-macromolecules , therefore could be apt for metabolomic analysis. Recent research on proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1HNMR)-based urinary metabolomics recruited 16 healthy volunteers and 8 IBS-D patients and indicated lower concentration of indoxyl-sulphate and increase of methylamine and taurine in IBS-D . Another study recruited 76 IBS participants at different time points and detected 10 me- tabolites consistently elevated in IBS, including a series of hydroxylysine metabolites, amino acids and SCFA de- rivatives . Here our data harvested 114 differentiated metabolites (50 with KEGG ID annotation) between IBS-D patients and HCs, demonstrating higher sensitiv- ity of UHPLC-MS/MS-based metabolomics (relevant studies listed in Table S6).

bioprojects.title: Lactose drives Enterococcus expansion to promote graft-versus-host disease
bioprojects.summary: The study investigates how lactose promotes Enterococcus expansion, exacerbating graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) after allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT). Using 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples from 1325 patients across four centers, the research found high Enterococcus abundance post-transplant, linked to increased GVHD severity and mortality. Dietary lactose depletion reduced Enterococcus growth in mice, while lactose-malabsorber genotypes impaired post-antibiotic clearance. The study highlights lactose as a key nutrient driving dysbiosis and inflammatory disease progression.

bioprojects.title: Infant gut microbiome composition is associated with non-social fear behavior in a pilot study
bioprojects.summary: This pilot study investigates the association between infant gut microbiome composition and non-social fear behavior. The research identifies specific bacterial taxa (e.g., Bacteroides, Veillonella) linked to fear responses, using Weighted Unifrac analysis. Findings suggest a potential relationship between gut microbiota and fear-related brain structures, though larger cohorts are needed for validation.
bioprojects.study_title: Infant gut microbiome composition is associated with non-social fear behavior in a pilot study
bioprojects.experimental_design: Pilot study with 34 infants assessing gut microbiome and fear behavior
bioprojects.funding_sources: NIH Grants T32 NS007432 and T32 GM008719, NSF GRFP Fellowship DGE-1650116
bioprojects.analysis_tools: Weighted Unifrac, linear mixed effects models
bioprojects.study_limitations: Small cohort, requires further validation
bioprojects.sample_size_justification: Pilot study with 34 infants; small cohort

entities.context: Interestingly, a prior study of preterm infants found that larger newborn amygdala volume was associated with increased escape behavior in response to non-social fear at 1 year83. Larger basolateral amygdala volumes are also associated with increased levels of anxiety later in development (around 8 years of age)84. In our secondary analysis of genera, 1-month Streptococcus relative abundance had a signiﬁcant negative association with 1-month amygdala volume after FDR correction. Our results parallel preclinical literature demonstrating the impact of the microbiome on morphology of the amygdala31 and clinical studies showing that functional connectivity of the amygdala is associated with the microbiome at 1 year of age85. Future studies using functional connectivity or diffusion tensor imaging to assess connectivity between these brain regions involved in fear may yield more insight.

entities.context: This dis- crepancy may be explained by the successional timing of gut microbiome development during infancy. The microbiome starts with a mix of aerotolerant bacteria like Lactobacillus, followed by transitions to facultative and obligate anaerobes62–64. Over the ﬁrst year, oxygen concentration in the gut lumen declines sig- niﬁcantly due to colonocyte metabolism of short chain fatty acids and luminal lipid oxidation65,66. This shapes the microbiome community by selecting for strict anaerobes like Bacteroides which can better tolerate increasingly anoxic conditions. Conse- quently, infants on the positive side of PC1 may have a relatively more mature gut microbiome due to the lower abundance of Lactobacillus and increased abundance of Bacteroides.
entities.definition: Metabolic byproducts of microbial fermentation in the gut

entities.context: The studies reviewed above suggest that the infant gut microbiome may be a key component in the normal development of fear behavior and associated brain structures. In addition, it may have a role in subsequent psychopathology, since fear behavior represents a fundamental behavioral dimension that is disrupted in multiple psychiatric disorders. Altered microbial composition has been reported in individuals with generalized anxiety disorder, autism, depression, schizophrenia, attention deﬁcit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and eating disorders43–47. A meta-analysis of probiotic interventions48 suggests positive effects on anxiety symptoms, and transplant of microbial com- munities from people with psychiatric illnesses into rodent models can induce relevant behaviors not seen when microbial communities from healthy controls are transplanted22,49–53. However, to date, there have been no studies testing the asso- ciation of the gut microbiome with observed fear behavior and fear-related brain structures during early human development.

bioprojects.title: Lifestyle and the presence of helminths is associated with gut microbiome composition in Cameroonians
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the relationship between lifestyle, helminth presence, and gut microbiome composition in 575 Cameroonian individuals. Using 16S rRNA amplicon and shotgun metagenomic sequencing, it finds that subsistence strategies (pastoralist, agropastoralist, hunter-gatherer) and parasite burden significantly influence microbial diversity. Helminth infections correlate with higher gut microbial diversity and immune responses, while dietary practices like milk consumption in Fulani pastoralists are linked to specific bacterial taxa. The study highlights the interplay between host lifestyle, microbiota, and immunity.
bioprojects.study_title: Lifestyle and the presence of helminths is associated with gut microbiome composition in Cameroonians
bioprojects.sample_source: Cameroon (Northwest, South, and East regions)
bioprojects.experimental_design: Comparative analysis of gut microbiome in Cameroonian populations with different lifestyles and parasite burdens
bioprojects.library_strategy: 16S rRNA amplicon and shotgun metagenomic sequencing
bioprojects.confounding_factors: Subsistence strategy, diet (e.g., milk consumption in Fulani), parasite presence, and lifestyle (pastoralist vs. urban)
bioprojects.analysis_tools: MAFFT, FastTree, Trimmomatic, Kraken 2, phyloseq, vegan, edgeR
bioprojects.study_limitations: Limited to Cameroonian populations; no long-term follow-up

entities.context: Here, we compared functional measures of the ability to breakdown milk sugars with microbiome data for Cameroonians, which includes a pastoralist population. The ability to break down lactose milk sugar in the small intestine past weaning and into adulthood is known as the lactase persistence (LP) phenotype [ 51]. We predicted that hosts who are lactase non-persistent (LNP) would not be capable of metabolizing lactose in the small intestine, and instead, the lactose would be catabolized by bacteria containing the LAC operon in the distal colon. The LAC operon, which produces beta- galactosidase, cleaves the milk sugar lactose into galactose and glucose, and gut bacteria with this operon may play a role in the digestion of dairy products (Additional file 1: Figure S15). We administered a lactose-tolerance test (LTT) to 154 Cameroonians to test for the association of the gut microbiome with the LP/LNP phenotype.

bioprojects.title: Compositional flux within the intestinal microbiota and risk for bloodstream infection with gram-negative bacteria
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the relationship between intestinal microbiota composition and the risk of gram-negative bloodstream infections in patients undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT). Using 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples, it identifies that Gram-negative bacterial domination (relative abundance ≥30%) predicts bloodstream infection. Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis reduces infections by limiting Gram-negative colonization, while initial colonization by Ruminococcaceae and Bacteroidetes offers protection. The study highlights dynamic microbiota changes during allo-HCT and their clinical implications.

bioprojects.title: Minor compositional alterations in faecal microbiota after five weeks and five months storage at room temperature on filter papers
bioprojects.summary: This study evaluates the impact of long-term room temperature (RT) storage on faecal microbiota composition using FOBT cards. The research found minimal compositional changes over five weeks and five months, with alpha-diversity remaining unaffected. Beta-diversity analysis showed host factors explained 65% of variation, while storage methods accounted for 5%. Single taxa analysis revealed significant alterations in four genera after five weeks and five after five months, but these were only detectable in fresh-frozen samples. The study concludes that FOBT card storage is viable for microbiota research.

entities.context: Faecal occult blood test (FOBT) papers are an appealing solution in such situations, and most studies find these to be applicable, showing no major changes within 7 days storage at room temperature (RT). As fieldwork often requires RT storage for longer periods, evaluation of this is warranted. We performed 16S rRNA gene sequencing of 19 paired faecal samples immediately frozen or kept five weeks and five months at RT on FOBT papers. Alpha-diversity evaluation revealed no effect of FOBT storage, and evaluation of beta-diversity showed that host explained 65% of community variation, while storage method explained 5%. Evaluation of community dispersion and the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio revealed a larger effect of storage time for fresh-frozen samples.

bioprojects.title: A prebiotic-enhanced lipid-based nutrient supplement (LNSp) increases Bifidobacterium relative abundance and enhances short-chain fatty acid production in simulated colonic microbiota from undernourished infants
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the impact of a prebiotic-enriched lipid-based nutrient supplement (LNSp) on gut microbiota composition and metabolic activity in undernourished infants using a dynamic human gut model (SHIME). LNSp significantly increased Bifidobacterium abundance, enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, and reduced pathogenic bacteria compared to standard LNS. The findings suggest that prebiotic-modified supplements could improve microbiota functionality in undernourished children, though further in vivo validation is needed.

entities.context: Prevotella is associated with plant rich diet and was found to be predominant in children from Burkina Faso . However, some Prevotella species, together with Acinetobacter and Mitsuokella are also found at high abundances in chronic inflammation status . Undernutrition, especially in its chronic form, is associated with environmental or tropical enteropathy, a condition character- ized by chronic intestinal inflammation and impaired intestinal barrier function . In this context, whether the high abundance of genus Prevotella in African children in gen- eral, and in the infants sampled for the present experiment in particular, is linked to plant based diet or to a subclinical intesti- nal inflammation status remains to be investigated. Our study also revealed LNSp to result in a significant decrease in the relative abundance of OTUs belonging to the gen- era Veillonella, Bilophila and Bacteroides, and in a delayed manner, of bacteria ascribed to the family Enterobacteriaceae.

entities.context: org/0000-0002-4472-6810 ABSTRACT Undernutrition remains a public health problem in the developing world with an attributable under-five death proportion of 45%. Lower gut microbiota diversity and poor metabolic output are associated with undernutrition and new therapeutic paths may come from steering gut microbiota composition and functionality. Using a dynamic gut model, the Simulator of Human Intestinal Microbial Ecosystem (SHIME R⃝), we investigated the effect of a lipid-based nutrient supplement enriched with prebiotics (LNSp), compared to LNS alone and control treatment, on the composition and metabolic functionality of fecal microbiota from three infants suffering from undernutrition. LNS elicited a significant increase in acetate and branched-chain fatty acid production, and a higher relative abundance of the genera Prevotella, Megasphaera, Acinetobacter, Acidaminococcus and Pseudomonas. In contrast, LNSp treatment resulted in a significant 9-fold increase in Bifidobacterium relative abundance and a decrease in that of potential pathogens and detrimental bacteria such as Enterobacteriaceae spp.
entities.definition: A simulated human intestinal microbiology model for in vitro studies.

Alpha diversity was computed and compared between treat- ment conditions using linear mixed models. A rarefaction to even depth was done to normalize sam- pling effort before comparing communities. Beta diversity was assessed based on the Bray–Curtis dissimilarity measure and visualized using non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) and heatmaps. Differences in acetate, propionate, butyrate and BCFA production between treatment conditions were assessed using linear mixed models. A stepwise model selection was done using a parametric bootstrapping to deter- mine the best model fits to the data, and when the result was not conclusive, the Akaike information criterion was used. Mod- els’ goodness of fit were post-hoc checked by plotting residual Q–Q plots. Predicted marginal means were then computed con- trasting all levels of treatment groups with a Tukey family-wise α correction for multiple comparisons.

bioprojects.title: Whole-Virome Analysis Sheds Light on Viral Dark Matter in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the human gut virome in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) using whole-virome analysis. It identifies shifts in viral composition, including a replacement of virulent bacteriophages with temperate ones in IBD patients. The research highlights the importance of gene-based clustering to address inter-individual variation and demonstrates that combining bacteriome and virome data improves disease classification. Findings suggest that viral dark matter plays a critical role in gut microbiome dynamics, offering potential biomarkers for IBD.

entities.context: Strain-level resolution hampers cohort comparisons due to a lack of shared sequences across subjects in the dataset, thereby masking compositional patterns occurring at higher taxonomic ranks across cohorts. Our initial analysis was carried out using VLSs (VLSs made non-redundant at 90% identity over 90% of the length), but this level of resolution did not reveal shared signals across co- horts. We overcame this issue by clustering viral genomes based on their protein-coding gene content using vConTACT2 . This gene network clustering approach re- vealed shared virome features while retaining relevant biological signals across the cohort (as seen by VCs across subjects), increased the variation explained in the b diversity, and decreased the abundance of unique viral VCs per subject across the dataset. Viral clustering also enabled the detection of a core virome in healthy subjects consisting of eight VCs across >50% of the cohort.

bioprojects.title: Long-Term Effects of Multi-Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis Treatment on Gut Microbiota and Its Health Consequences
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the long-term effects of multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) treatment on gut microbiota and health outcomes. Using fecal and blood samples from 76 participants, including an active MDR-TB group, a recovered group, and two treatment-naive controls, the research found persistent gut microbiota dysbiosis even 3–8 years post-treatment. Despite no observed gastrointestinal symptoms, lipid profile changes (e.g., elevated LDL-C and TC) were linked to altered bacterial taxa. The study highlights the lasting impact of MDR-TB therapy on microbial communities and metabolic health.

entities.context: In 2016, 490,000 new cases of MDR-TB occurred . MDR-TB treatment consists of a variety of narrow-spectrum and broad-spectrum antibiotics and lasts for at least 20 months. A course of treatment consists of an 8-month intensive treatment with one injection drug from kanamycin, amikacin or capreomycin, and four oral drugs from ﬁrst-line drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, rifabutin, and rifapentine), ﬂuoroquinolones (levoﬂoxacin, moxiﬂoxacin, and gatiﬂoxacin) and second- line oral bacteriostatic drugs (ethionamide, prothionamide, cycloserine, terizidone, para-aminosalicylic acid, and para- aminosalicylate sodium). Then the administration of the four oral antibiotic drugs continues for another 12 months . Gut microbiota plays an important role in human health, involving in the development of immune system, the regulation of metabolism, the protection from pathogen overgrowth, the regulation of intestinal endocrine hormone, the biosynthesis of vitamins and the provision of energy .
entities.definition: Antibiotic used in MDR-TB treatment

entities.context: The antibiotic-induced gut microbiota dysbiosis has adverse health consequences, including metabolic disorder, allergy, inﬂammatory bowel disease, and infectious disease . Epidemiological studies suggested an association between antibiotic exposure and an increased risk of obesity and diabetes . Rodent research also found that antibiotic exposure led to increased adiposity with up-regulated lipogenesis and triglyceride (TG) synthesis . The fecal transplantation from antibiotic-treated mice into germ-free mice led to higher fat mass compared with the fecal transplantation from mice without antibiotic treatment, suggesting the role of gut microbiota in the antibiotic-induced adiposity . In addition, gut microbiota interacts with the immune system to ensure proper diﬀerentiation and complete development of immunity .

bioprojects.title: Development of the gut microbiota in early life: The impact of cystic fibrosis and antibiotic treatment
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the development of gut microbiota in infants with Cystic Fibrosis (CF) compared to healthy controls, focusing on the effects of CFTR dysfunction and antibiotic use. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, it identifies significant differences in microbial composition, including reduced diversity and altered bacterial abundances in CF infants. The research highlights that antibiotic treatment exacerbates microbiota dysbiosis, with implications for gut health and potential therapeutic strategies.

Using a Smoothing Spline Analysis of Vari- ance (SS-ANOVA,R-package: ﬁtTimeSeries), periods were identiﬁed during which the alpha-diversity was signiﬁcantly different be- tween healthy infants and infants with CF Mean relative abun- dances for the most abundant OTU’s were calculated per month for healthy and control samples. To determine speciﬁc periods during which genera were differentially present in healthy and CF sam- ples, the read counts were normalized using metagenomeSeq and an SS-ANOVA was performed (R-package: ﬁtTimeSeries) The Benjamini Hochberg procedure was used to correct for multiple testing . A non-metric dimensional scaling (nMDS) plot was made to visualise the diversity of the overall microbial composi- tion (R-package: Vegan). This non-parametric method is used for dimension reduction, whereby per sample the complete microbiota composition is depicted as a single point in a two-dimensional space.

entities.context: A den- drogram of all samples was constructed using the Bray-Curtis dis- similarity, with the optimal number of clusters deﬁned by the Sil- houette index (R-package: cluster). Differences between the num- ber of CF and control samples within clusters were tested using chi-square tests, and corrected for multiple testing with the Ben- jamini Hochberg procedure. To visualize gut microbiota develop- ment in children over time an alluvial plot was constructed using the Alluvial package in R (R-package: Alluvial). The microbial sta- bility over time was evaluated using the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between consecutive samples from the same child. A linear mixed effects model of these Bray-Curtis dissimilarities was used to de- termine the difference in stability between infants with CF and healthy infant over time.

bioprojects.title: Enterobacterales Infection after Intestinal Dominance in Hospitalized Patients
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the association between Enterobacterales intestinal dominance and subsequent infections in hospitalized patients. The research develops a PCR-based assay to measure Enterobacterales density, validates it against 16S rRNA sequencing, and finds that both absolute and relative abundance correlate with infection risk. The findings suggest qPCR is feasible for clinical use, highlighting the potential for infection prevention strategies targeting microbial colonization.

DISCUSSION The aims of this study were to develop a qPCR assay to measure Enterobacterales abundance on rectal swabs, validate this PCR assay against 16S rRNA sequence analysis as the gold standard, and measure the association between Enterobacterales abun- dance and subsequent infection. Towards these aims, we developed and validated two real-time PCR assays that measure Enterobacterales as a proportion of total bacterial 16S rRNA-encoding DNA in a sample. These assays are somewhat complementary, as assay A had better analytical performance in terms of precision, linearity, and reportable range, but assay B was inclusive of Bacteroides species.

bioprojects.title: Featured Gut Microbiomes Associated With the Progression of Chronic Hepatitis B Disease
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates gut microbiota dysbiosis in chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) progression. Using 16S rRNA sequencing of 400 fecal samples, it identifies bacterial taxa shifts associated with disease stages (healthy → CHB → liver cirrhosis). Key findings include increased Fusobacteria/Actinobacteria and decreased Prevotella in diseased states, with diagnostic potential via OTU networks. The research highlights microbiota's role in HBV pathogenesis and suggests therapeutic targets.

entities.context: Approximately 400 fecal samples were collected, and 97 samples were subjected to 16S rRNA gene sequencing after age and BMI matching. Compared with the healthy individuals, signiﬁcant gut microbiota alterations were associated with the progression of liver disease. LEfSe results showed that the HBV infected patients had higher Fusobacteria, Veillonella, and Haemophilus abundance while the healthy individuals had higher levels of Prevotella and Phascolarctobacterium. Indicator analysis revealed that 57 OTUs changed as the disease progressed, and their combination produced an AUC value of 90% (95% CI: 86–94%) between the LC and non-LC groups. In addition, the abundances of OTU51 (Dialister succinatiphilus) and OTU50 (Alistipes onderdonkii) decreased as the disease progressed, and these results were further veriﬁed by qPCR.
entities.definition: A genus of bacteria commonly found in the human gut microbiota

entities.context: Previous studies indicate that compositional changes of the gut microbiota are closely related to chronic liver diseases, such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) , non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) , alcoholic liver disease (ALD) , hepatic encephalopathy (HE) , cirrhosis , hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) , and HBV infection. Increasing evidence suggests that the gut microbiota has evolved as a new important player in the pathogenesis of hepatitis B virus-induced chronic liver disease. A variety of gut commensals, such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Enterococcus faecalis, Enterobacteriaceae, Biﬁdobacteria, and lactic acid bacteria (Lactobacillus, Pediococcus, Leuconostoc, and Weissella), are known to be diﬀerent in the intestine of HBV cirrhotic patients . We have previously induced hepatitis B virus e-Antigen (HBeAg) clearance in patients with positive HBeAg after undergoing long-term antiviral therapy through several fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) treatments, which were accompanied by signiﬁcant changes in the microbiota composition . bioprojects.title: Synbiotic Alters Fecal Microbiomes, but not Liver Fat or Fibrosis, in a Randomized Trial of Patients With Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
bioprojects.summary: This study investigated the effects of a synbiotic (probiotic and prebiotic) on liver fat, fibrosis, and fecal microbiomes in patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). A double-blind phase 2 trial of 104 UK patients found that the synbiotic altered gut microbiota composition, increasing Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium while reducing Oscillibacter and Alistipes. However, no significant reduction in liver fat or fibrosis markers was observed. The study highlights the potential of synbiotics to modulate microbiomes without impacting liver pathology.

bioprojects.title: US nativity and dietary acculturation impact the gut microbiome in a diverse US population
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates how immigrant acculturation and US nativity influence gut microbiome composition. Using 16S rRNA sequencing of stool samples from 863 US residents (including foreign-born Koreans and Hispanics, and US-born Whites/Blacks), it identifies distinct microbial profiles associated with dietary acculturation. Key findings include enrichment of seaweed-degrading Bacteroides plebeius in foreign-born Koreans and Prevotella copri in acculturated immigrants, suggesting that dietary changes during acculturation alter microbiome diversity. The study concludes that US nativity and dietary adaptation significantly shape the gut microbiome.

entities.context: We characterized differences in the gut microbiome between racially/ethnically diverse US immigrant and US-born groups, and determined the impact of dietary acculturation on the microbiome. Stool samples were collected from 863 US residents, including US-born (315 White, 93 Black, 40 Hispanic) and foreign-born (105 Hispanic, 264 Korean) groups. We determined dietary acculturation from dissimilarities based on food frequency questionnaires, and used 16S rRNA gene sequencing to characterize the microbiome. Gut microbiome composition differed across study groups, with the largest difference between foreign-born Koreans and US-born Whites, and signiﬁcant differences also observed between foreign-born and US-born Hispanics. Differences in sub- operational taxonomic unit (s-OTU) abundance between foreign-born and US-born groups tended to be distinct from differences between US-born groups.

bioprojects.title: Topical emollient therapy with sunflower seed oil alters the skin microbiota of young children with severe acute malnutrition in Bangladesh: A randomised, controlled study
bioprojects.summary: The study investigates how topical sunflower seed oil (SSO) affects the skin and gut microbiota of children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM). Using 16S rRNA sequencing, it found SSO therapy significantly altered skin microbiota diversity and composition across multiple body sites, including untreated areas like the forehead. Gut microbiota showed associations with age and sampling day but no significant treatment effect. The research suggests SSO may improve skin barrier function through microbial changes and systemic mechanisms.

entities.context: Assessment of impact of emollient therapy on skin and gut microbiota diversity Linear mixed-effects modelling was used to assess the association between the Shannon diversity index and study group. Because of study design and the concurrent clinical need for administration of antibiotics to treat the combination of SAM and acute diarrhea, we considered the effects of emollient on the microbiota con- founded by the effects of antibiotics which are a potent form of microbiota perturbation. Models were fit using the lmer function in the lme4 package (version 1.1.0) and built following the principle of parsimony using a forward-selection approach with variables – study group, sample day, skin site, age, sex, antibiotics, delivery mode, breastfeeding – sequentially added to identify the best fitting model.

bioprojects.title: Distinct Polysaccharide Utilization Profiles of Human Intestinal Prevotella copri Isolates
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the genomic and functional diversity of 83 Prevotella copri isolates from 11 human donors. The research highlights extensive genome variation, including distinct clades and differences in susC genes and PULs (polysaccharide utilization loci). In vitro experiments demonstrate that these isolates utilize unique sets of plant-derived polysaccharides, distinguishing them from animal-based sources. The findings reveal genomic and functional diversity in human intestinal P. copri strains, with implications for diet-microbiome interactions and disease associations.

Although mechanistic models of metabolism, growth, and colonization have been established for several in- testinal Bacteroides and oral Prevotella spp., studies of intestinal Prevotella have lacked experimental tools and relied heavily on only two type strains, Prevotella copri and Prevotella stercorea . Many researchers have observed Prevotella’s presence and abundance by using 16S sequencing, but its genomic diversity and biological properties have not been described. Because Prevotella copri are highly sensitive to oxygen, and difﬁcult to isolate and cultivate, previous studies have been limited to the single commercially available type strain, DSM 18205, to perform metagenomic comparisons and draw experimental conclusions.

entities.context: INTRODUCTION Humans live in close association with a teeming bacterial ecosystem known as the gut microbiome. The diverse inhabi- tants of this extraordinary environment perform beneﬁcial and remarkable services for their host, out-competing harmful bacte- ria and digesting the majority of dietary ﬁber . The relative abundance of two genera, Bacteroides and Prevotella, is inversely correlated in the intestine . bioprojects.title: Precision Microbiome Modulation with Discrete Dietary Fiber Structures Directs Short-Chain Fatty Acid Production
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates how discrete dietary fiber (DF) structures influence gut microbiome composition and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production. Using a dose-response trial with three type-IV resistant starches (RS4s), the research demonstrates that structural differences in DFs lead to specific shifts in microbial communities, directing SCFA output toward propionate or butyrate. Key findings include dose-dependent effects plateauing at 35 g/day and consistent microbiome responses within treatment groups. The study highlights the potential for targeted microbiome modulation via structurally defined DFs.

In vitro and in vivo studies have shown that struc- tural differences of DFs dictate the microbes involved in their degradation and the effects on the bacterial community, which are often speciﬁc yet difﬁcult to predict . Fermentation of DF produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs; acetate, propionate, and butyrate), which are largely considered beneﬁcial but differ in their physiological ef- fects . Mechanistic studies in animal models showed beneﬁcial effects of butyrate in maintaining GI barrier integrity, quenching oxygen at the epithelial interface, and exert- ing immune-modulating effects , while propionate has been shown to induce satiety through induction of anorectic hormones and intestinal gluconeogenesis (IGN), which also inﬂuences glucose meta- bolism . Direct evi- dence in humans is limited, but butyrate is considered to be anti-carcinogenic and anti-inﬂammatory , while propionate has been shown to induce satiety and improve glucose metabolism .

entities.context: From a more practical perspective, the exact DF dose required for reliable changes, and if such doses are tolerable by modern-day humans, is unknown . All these factors question whether discrete DF structures could be used to induce targeted and predictable alterations in humans. In this study, we tested the hypothesis that small discrete differ- ences in the chemical structure of DF can be used to direct changes in fecal microbiota composition and its functions. To achieve this, we performed a randomized controlled trial in hu- mans to compare the effects and dose-response relationships of three type-IV resistant starches (RS4s) on fecal microbiota composition, SCFA proﬁles, and perceived GI tolerance. RSs were chosen as the DF source because they have well character- ized, substrate-speciﬁc effects on the human gut microbiome , while the use of RS4s with well-characterized chemical modiﬁcations allowed the elucidation of speciﬁc structure-func- tion relationships between DF and the microbiome.

bioprojects.title: Spatial and temporal modulation of enterotoxigenic E. coli H10407 pathogenesis and interplay with microbiota in human gut models
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the spatial-temporal dynamics of enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) H10407 survival, virulence, and interactions with gut microbiota using in vitro models (TIM-1 and M-SHIME). Key findings include ETEC viability loss during gastric digestion, growth renewal in jejunal/ileal phases, and modulation of microbial communities. The research highlights the role of gastrointestinal cues in ETEC pathogenesis and suggests implications for developing prophylactic strategies against diarrheal diseases.

entities.context: Conclusions To conclude, ETEC pathogenesis in the human gastro- intestinal tract was thus far considered a “black box.” Our present study provided for the first time a detailed insight into the temporal and spatial modulation of ETEC H10407 survival, virulence, and its interactions with gut microbes by combining the two most complete and well-validated TIM-1 and M-SHIME systems world- wide. Future results will enable prospecting of preventive and/or therapeutic strategies. entities.context: In addition, only three recent studies have ex- plored the human gut microbiota changes during the initiation and progression of ETEC diarrhea [9–11]. No data are available on how the human gut microbiota may influence ETEC survival and virulence. The few studies available all relied on fecal samples and rectal swabs collected from patients that experienced an ETEC episode, or in the course of a clinical trial where healthy adults have been challenged with an infra-physiological dose of ETEC [9–11]. However, it is generally accepted that fecal microbial communities fundamentally differ from microbial communities residing in other locations in the gastrointestinal tract. Therefore, integration and sequential delivery of gastrointestinal signals are needed to model the dynam- ics and complexity of the human gut more closely as well as to investigate ETEC behavior in different gastro- intestinal environments.

bioprojects.title: A Critical Mutualism – Competition Interplay Underlies the Loss of Microbial Diversity in Sedentary Lifestyle
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates how sedentary lifestyles correlate with reduced gut microbial diversity and altered interaction networks. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, it found that sedentary individuals had lower microbiota diversity and network complexity compared to active individuals. Competitive interactions were higher in active groups, and the mutualism-competition ratio was linked to diversity loss in sedentary populations.

entities.context: Notably, our topological measure was based on the complexity of the network, also called cohesion , and not simply the degree, strength, or number of connections. We chose a topological measure to extend the meaning of an intricate relationship. The decrease in the network cohesion occurs by aﬀecting selective species, not in a uniform way but by decreasing the nested nature of the competitive network. Natural networks are proposed to not be random; but rather to display a nestedness or modular structure that is related to the stability and dynamics of the ecosystem . The loss of modularity or nestedness behavior generally entails a reduction in richness or topological eﬃciency , as well as eﬀective interspeciﬁc competition.

entities.context: This phenomenon has important implications for treatment tests, because the variance of a subset of bacteria can predict the behavior of others. In the case, for example, of antibiotic intake, given the decrease of some bacterial species due to the eﬀect of the drug, one could better predict what would happen to the other bacteria in the sedentary population. If there is more diversity, as in active population, there is a greater probability of ﬁnding more ways to recover the allostatic balance. Therefore, the variance of the species that are not aﬀected by the drug will be less predictable. With reduced diversity, the ecosystem has less regulatory capacity because species can be controlled.

entities.context: The goal of this study was to determine whether individuals with a sedentary lifestyle have lower diversity in their gut microbiota and how microbial diversity is associated with changes in bacterial network interactions. For that purpose, diet, body composition, physical activity, and sedentarism behavior were characterized for individuals who did or did not comply with the World Health Organization recommendations for physical activity. The composition of the gut microbiome was determined by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Reorganization of microbial structure with lifestyle was approached from network analysis, where network complexity and the topology of positive and negative interdependences between bacteria were compared and correlated with microbial diversity. Sedentary lifestyle was signiﬁcantly associated with a diet low in ﬁber and rich in sugars and processed meat, as well as with high visceral and total corporal fat composition.

Sedentarism: Loss of Competition and Microbial Diversity INTRODUCTION The gut microbiota has emerged as an important factor in human health and disease. Indeed, speciﬁc microbial patterns have been associated with numerous disorders, such as cancer or cardiovascular disease . Numerous studies that compare the gut microbiota in health and disease point to the loss of microbial diversity as a disease characteristic. For instance, patients with ileal Crohn’s disease, irritable bowel syndrome or rheumatoid arthritis, have lower microbiota diversity compared to their healthy peers .

bioprojects.title: Gut microbiota modulation with long-chain corn bran arabinoxylan in adults with overweight and obesity is linked to an individualized temporal increase in fecal propionate
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates how long-chain arabinoxylan affects gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production in overweight/obese adults. A randomized controlled trial with 31 participants showed that arabinoxylan altered fecal bacterial communities, reduced alpha diversity, increased propionate levels, and revealed individualized responses linked to baseline microbiota composition. The findings highlight the importance of ecological frameworks for predicting dietary fiber fermentation outcomes.

Overall, our findings suggest that arabinoxylan has prebiotic properties in that it promotes putatively health-related organisms and the production of propion- ate, making it a promising candidate for the prevention of obesity and associated pathologies, especially if its ap- plication is personalized. bioprojects.title: A Calcium-Rich Multimineral Intervention to Modulate Colonic Microbial Communities and Metabolomic Profiles in Humans: Results from a 90-Day Trial
bioprojects.summary: This study investigated the effects of Aquamin, a calcium-magnesium-rich multimineral supplement, on colonic microbial communities and metabolomic profiles in 30 healthy human participants over 90 days. Compared to calcium alone or placebo, Aquamin significantly reduced total bacterial DNA and altered microbial composition (thetaYC; P=0.0087), decreased bile acid levels (P=0.0375), and increased short-chain fatty acid acetate (P<0.0001). The intervention was safe with no serious adverse events, but findings are preliminary due to the small sample size.

entities.context: Introduction Epidemiologic studies have shown an inverse relationship between calcium intake and colon cancer incidence (1). Exper- imental studies in animals have substantiated antitumor efﬁ- cacy in the colon (2), and in vitro studies have provided mechanistic insight into how calcium inﬂuences epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation (3). In spite of these data, interventional trials with calcium have had only modest success in reducing colon polyp formation, with some trials demon- strating a reduction in incidence (4, 5), while others showing essentially no protection (6, 7) or an increase in incidence of colon polyps with a more-aggressive sessile-serrated pheno- type (8). This complicated picture supports the idea that adequate or optimal calcium intake throughout life may be beneﬁcial, but in a realistic dietary setting, the efﬁcacy of supplementation by calcium alone may be limited by dietary complexity. Potentially adverse effects at higher dose levels further complicate the picture (9).

bioprojects.title: Gut microbiota composition during infancy and subsequent behavioural outcomes
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the relationship between gut microbiota composition in infancy and behavioral outcomes at age 2. A subcohort of 201 children was analyzed, showing an association between reduced Prevotella abundance at 12 months and increased behavioral problems. The findings highlight the importance of antibiotic use in early life and suggest implications for gut-brain axis research.

bioprojects.title: Breastfeeding restored the gut microbiota in caesarean section infants and lowered the infection risk in early life
bioprojects.summary: This study investigated how delivery mode (caesarean section vs. vaginal delivery) and feeding patterns (breastfeeding vs. formula milk) affect neonatal gut microbiota (GM) development. Using 207 faecal samples from 41 infants collected at six time points, the research identified three GM patterns and found that CS infants had lower Bifidobacterium abundance, which was partially restored by breastfeeding. This restoration correlated with reduced respiratory and diarrhoeal infections in early life.
bioprojects.study_title: Breastfeeding restored the gut microbiota in caesarean section infants and lowered the infection risk in early life
bioprojects.sample_source: Third Hospital of Hebei Medical University

entities.context: The infants were assigned to four groups according to delivery mode (caesarean section (CS) or vaginal delivery (VD)) and feeding pattern (breastfeeding or formula milk). Results: The meconium bacterial diversity was slightly higher in CS than in VD. Three GM patterns were identified, including Escherichia/Shigella-Streptococcus-dominated, Bifidobacterium-Escherichia/Shigella-dominated and Bifidobacterium-dominated patterns, and they gradually changed over time. In CS infants, Bifidobacterium was less abundant, and the delay in GM establishment could be partially restored by breastfeeding. The frequency of respiratory tract infection and diarrhoea consequently decreased.

bioprojects.title: The influence of blood on the human gut microbiome
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates how blood in stools affects gut microbiome composition, independent of colorectal cancer (CRC). Using iFOBT screening data from 500 patients, researchers identified 12 bacterial species whose abundance significantly differed between groups with and without blood in stools. The findings suggest that blood itself alters microbiome signatures, highlighting the need to account for blood presence in microbiome research related to intestinal diseases.

We used the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity to quantify the dissimilarity be- tween two samples using not only the presence of an element but also its abundance within the sample. Differentially abundant taxa using LEfSe For these analyses, we removed all OTUs present in less than 10% of our study population, merged OTUs at the species level and converted the read count to relative abundances. To identify differentially abundant taxa be- tween patients with positive and negative iFOBT results we used the biomarker discovery algorithm LEfSe . LEfSe identifies features with are statistically different between conditions by first using a non-parametric Kruskal Wallis sum-rank test followed by a pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum test on the features that were significant in the previous step.

entities.context: Results: We observed significant differences in the intestinal bacterial composition that could be solely caused by the presence of blood in stools. More precisely, we identified 12 bacterial species showing significant differences in abundance between both our study groups. These species, Bacteroides uniformis, Collinsella aerofaciens, Eggerthella lenta and Clostridium symbiosum demonstrated increased abundance in the presence of blood. In contrast, the species Prevotella copri, Coprococcus eutactus and catus, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Roseburia faecis, Blautia obeum, Gemmiger formicilis and Clostridium celatum showed decreased abundance in patients with blood in their stools. Notably, we found multiple taxa that were reported in previous studies linking microbiome composition and diseases.
entities.definition: A bacterial species associated with increased abundance in the presence of blood in stools

Keywords: Gut microbiota, Colorectal cancer, Blood, 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, Bacteria, Taxonomic biomarkers, LefSe, iFOBT testing Background The development of various diseases such as type 2 dia- betes, colorectal cancer (CRC), inflammatory bowel dis- eases and even depression, which is seemingly unrelated to the gut, has been discussed as being linked to the composition of the intestinal microbiome [1–9]. For ex- ample, Fusobacterium nucleatum has been identified as playing multiple roles in the development of CRC or its treatment , such as augmenting CRC cell prolifera- tion or increasing resistance to chemotherapy . Moreover, enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis and polyketide synthase-producing Escherichia coli have also been reported to promote colorectal cancer by pro- ducing DNA damaging molecules such as colobactin . Remarkably, even though the microbiome and hu- man health are tightly intertwined, the microbiome com- position remains underused as a biomarker of disease progression or in the diagnosis process.
entities.definition: A bacterial species linked to colorectal cancer and blood in stools

entities.context: Differently abundant taxa between patients with and without blood in their stool Using LEfSe (Linear discriminant analysis effect size) , we were able to identify taxa whose abundance dif- fered significantly between participants who did not have blood in their stool and their counterpart who did (Figs. 3 and 4). These results indicate that differences can be identified at all taxonomic levels from the phylum to the species and that they spread through all the phyla present in our analysis except for the Synergistetes and Verrucomicrobia phyla. The taxa with higher abundance in participants without blood are part of the Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes phylum and the only Archea phylum in our analysis (Euryarchaeota). bioprojects.title: Prospective study reveals a microbiome signature that predicts the occurrence of post-operative enterocolitis in Hirschsprung disease (HSCR) patients
bioprojects.summary: This prospective study identifies a gut microbiome signature predictive of post-operative Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC) in HSCR patients. The research found a 21-OTU microbial signature with ~85% accuracy for HAEC prediction, highlights exclusive breastfeeding as a protective factor linked to reduced Gram-negative bacteria and LPS levels, and suggests microbiome modulation via breastfeeding could prevent HAEC progression.

entities.context: Although we observed a higher abundance of Lactobacillus in the enteric microbiome of exclusively breastfed patients, no significant difference was observed between postoperative HAEC cases and controls. It is well known that lipopolysaccharide is pro- duced by Gram-negative bacteria.29,30 We performed KEGG pathway analysis and found significant enrichment for LPS biosynthesis proteins and secre- tion system in postoperative HAEC cases. Significant enrichment for LPS biosynthesis proteins and secre- tion system was also observed in patients without exclusive breastfeeding. ELISA with the homogenate of the enteric tissue in the cutting edge of the dilated segment confirmed that the level of LPS was increased in postoperative HAEC cases and decreased in the exclusive-breastfeeding group.

Identification of HAEC At the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University, diagnosis of HAEC was based on the criteria published by Pastor et al.,32 and documented by a physician (W.T.). A summary of the HAEC scoring system is presented in Table S6, and a score of 10 or greater resulted in the diagnosis of HAEC. Moreover, HSCR patients were asked to have follow- up visits in 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, and 3 years after surgery. On each visit, the physician asked if the patient had ever been diagnosed with HAEC by any hospital. Microbiome sequencing At the pull-through surgery, the cutting edge of dilated segments of HSCR patients was collected and immediately stored at −80°C. Our standard of exci- sion is to find mature ganglion cells on the cutting edge of the dilated segment based on fast pathology during surgery. Generally, the distance between the cutting edge of the dilated segment and the transi- tional segment is more than 10 cm. For classical segment HSCR, the cutting edge was usually located in the proximal sigmoid colon or the descending colon. For long-segment HSCR, the cutting edge reached the descending colon, the transverse colon, and sometimes the ascending colon. In the case of total colonic aganglionosis, the cutting edge reached the small intestine. We collected the enteric mucosa in the cutting edge of the dilated segment for sequen- cing, which is adjacent to normal tissue and thus better represents the characteristics of normal enteric tissues and anastomotic stoma after surgery. DNA in the enteric mucosa was extracted and purified by the GUT MICROBES QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (QIAGEN). The 16S rRNA gene was amplified by the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), using primers 515F (5′-GTGCCAGCMGC C

bioprojects.title: Systematic Analysis of Impact of Sampling Regions and Storage Methods on Fecal Gut Microbiome and Metabolome Proﬁles
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates how fecal sampling regions and storage conditions affect gut microbiome and metabolome profiles. It found that sampling regions had minimal impact on microbial diversity but significant variation in metabolites, while storage methods like RNALater caused notable changes. Short-term room temperature storage was less disruptive, and homogenization was critical for metabolomics but not microbiology. The research emphasizes standardized protocols for reliable large-scale studies.

entities.context: In this study, we systematically investi- gated the effects of fecal sampling regions and storage and retrieval conditions on gut microbiome and metabolite proﬁles from three healthy children. Our analysis in- dicated that compared to homogenized and snap-frozen samples (standard control [SC]), different sampling regions did not affect microbial community alpha diversity, while a total of 22 of 176 identiﬁed metabolites varied signiﬁcantly across different sampling regions. In contrast, storage conditions signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced the micro- biome and metabolome. Short-term room temperature storage had a minimal effect on the microbiome and metabolome proﬁles. Sample storage in RNALater showed a signiﬁcant level of variation in both microbiome and metabolome proﬁles, indepen- dent of the storage or retrieval conditions.
entities.definition: Environmental parameters affecting sample preservation

entities.context: Sample storage in RNALater showed a signiﬁcant level of variation in both microbiome and metabolome proﬁles, indepen- dent of the storage or retrieval conditions. The effect of RNALater on the metabo- lome was stronger than the effect on the microbiome, and individual variability be- tween study participants outweighed the effect of RNALater on the microbiome. We conclude that homogenizing stool samples was critical for metabolomic analysis but not necessary for microbiome analysis. Short-term room temperature storage had a minimal effect on the microbiome and metabolome proﬁles and is recommended for short-term fecal sample storage. In addition, our study indicates that the use of RNALater as a storage medium of stool samples for microbial and metabolomic anal- yses is not recommended.

bioprojects.title: HIV-associated gut dysbiosis is independent of sexual practice and correlates with noncommunicable diseases
bioprojects.summary: This study investigates the relationship between HIV infection, gut microbiota composition, and non-communicable diseases. It identifies distinct microbial signatures in antiretroviral-treated HIV-positive individuals compared to controls, highlighting persistent gut dysbiosis independent of sexual practices. The research links these microbial changes to systemic inflammation and age-related comorbidities, emphasizing the role of gut microbiota in HIV disease progression.

entities.context: We report that MSM harbor a markedly different gut micro- biota composition than that of MSW. Though HIV infection status exhibited a strong microbiota signature, the effect of MSM on the microbiota was more pronounced than that of HIV status by both numbers of ASVs that were in differential abundance and by robustness as assessed via machine learning analyses. We ﬁnd overlap between bacterial community shifts in MSM and MSM/ RAI+, supporting the idea that RAI represents a driving factor for microbiota differences observed between MSM and MSW. The lack of bacterial community differences between condomless MSM/RAI+ and MSM/RAI+ with condom suggests that the RAI-associated microbiota may not be an effect of semen but perhaps is linked with other practices associated with RAI, for example rectal douching and use of lubricants. Interestingly, the females who reported engaging in RAI bore compositional similarities to MSM/RAI+, indicating that RAI may be linked to a microbiota signature regardless of gender.
entities.definition: Recurrent Anal Infections, a clinical parameter associated with microbiota dysbiosis
entities.examples: ["RAI in HIV patients", "RAI as a marker of gut health"]
